title: Rust stains, cracks and falling chips of concrete: what spalling on your Florida condo building means
seoTitle: Florida Condo Spalling and Rebar Rust, Explained
description: What concrete spalling and rebar rust are, how Florida's milestone inspection law treats cracks, and what condo owners and boards can do when they see them.
dek: A brown stain under a balcony. A crack that keeps getting longer. A chunk of concrete on the walkway. Here is what those signs can mean, what Florida law says about them, and who to tell.
facebook: Ever spotted a rust stain under a balcony or a chip of concrete on the walkway and wondered if it matters? Here's what spalling is, why salt air and rusting steel cause it, and what Florida's milestone law says about cracks.

body.text: Most Florida condo buildings near the water are made of concrete with steel bars inside. That steel is what holds the concrete together when it bends or stretches. When the steel starts to rust, the building often shows it on the outside first.

Owners are usually the first to notice. You walk the same hallway and sit on the same balcony every day. This guide explains what those signs are, how Florida's milestone inspection law treats them, and who to tell. It is a guide, not engineering or legal advice. Only a licensed engineer or architect who has looked at your building can say what a crack means.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: Rebar: short for reinforcing bar, the steel rods set inside concrete. Spalling: when pieces of the concrete surface crack loose, flake off or fall away, often showing rusty steel underneath. Milestone inspection: the structural inspection Florida requires for condo buildings three habitable stories or taller, starting at 30 years old (or 25 where the local building office requires it) and every 10 years after. Phase 1 and Phase 2: the two parts of a milestone inspection. Phase 1 is a look-over. Phase 2 is a closer look, done only when Phase 1 finds trouble.

New concrete protects the steel inside it. A NASA article on concrete corrosion explains that fresh concrete has a high pH, which holds rust back. Over the years, salt and moisture work their way in. In NASA's words, "The salt migrates down to the steel reinforcing bars, rusting the bars and cracking the concrete."

Then it feeds on itself. The same article says cracks "allow more water, more salt, and more acid to enter," which leads to "larger cracks and spalling." That is why a small problem on a balcony edge rarely stays small on its own.

items: Brown or orange rust stains bleeding out of concrete, often on balcony edges, slab undersides, columns or around railing posts.
Cracks, especially ones that run in a line, get wider over time, or have rust in them.
Bulging, hollow-sounding or loose patches of concrete or stucco.
Chips or chunks of concrete on balconies, walkways or the ground below.
Steel bars you can actually see where concrete has fallen away.

body.text: None of these alone tells you how serious a problem is. Some are cosmetic. Some are not. That call belongs to an engineer or architect.
What Florida's milestone law says about cracks

Florida's milestone inspection law is section 553.899 of the 2026 Florida Statutes. It uses the phrase "substantial structural deterioration." The law defines that as "substantial structural distress or substantial structural weakness" that "negatively affects a building's general structural condition and integrity."

Here is the part owners often miss. The definition leaves out surface imperfections "such as cracks, distortion, sagging, deflections, misalignment," signs of leakage and peeling finishes. But it adds an exception: they count if the licensed engineer or architect doing the inspection decides they are a sign of substantial structural deterioration. So a crack is not automatically a structural problem, and it is not automatically harmless either.

In Phase 1, the engineer or architect does a visual examination of the building, including the major structural parts. If they find no signs of substantial structural deterioration, the law says Phase 2 is not required. If they do find it, Phase 2 must be done. The written report must identify any substantial structural deterioration, recommend repairs, and say whether unsafe or dangerous conditions were seen.

A recommended milestone report form prepared for the Florida Building Commission shows what inspectors write down. It asks about cracking, spalling and rebar corrosion. For balconies, it gives "minor cracking, minor rebar corrosion – patching will suffice" as an example of a Fair rating, and "significant cracking, rebar corrosion requiring repairs" as an example of a Poor rating.

In July 2026, the Legislature's research office, OPPAGA, published the first statewide look at milestone inspection data reported to the Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) for 2024 and 2025. Building officials reported 8,736 completed Phase 1 inspections and 1,575 completed Phase 2 inspections. They reported 903 permit applications for repairs found in Phase 2. Concrete was among the most common types of repair.
OPPAGA also notes the numbers are incomplete. DBPR got data from 71% of jurisdictions for 2024 and 64% for 2025.

items: Take a dated photo and write down exactly where it is: floor, unit, balcony, column or walkway.
Tell the board or the manager in writing, by email or letter, so there is a record. Ask that it be passed to the association's engineer.

Ask for the building's most recent milestone inspection summary. The law requires the association to give every owner a copy within 45 days after receiving the report, and to post it in a conspicuous place on the property.
If concrete is falling where people walk, say so plainly and right away. Keep clear of the area until someone qualified has looked at it.
Don't chip at it, patch it or paint over it yourself. Covering a stain can hide what the engineer needs to see. Ask the board first.

body.text: If you are on the board:

items: Keep owner reports in the association's records, with photos and dates.
Send them to the engineer or architect who did your milestone inspection or SIRS, and ask whether anything needs a closer look before the next scheduled inspection.
Ask the engineer what, if anything, should be done about access to an area while it is being evaluated.

If a Phase 2 report recommends repairs, Florida law says they must be commenced within 365 days after the association receives the report. Talk with the engineer and the association attorney about the schedule.
If anyone believes a condition is unsafe, tell the engineer and contact the local building department, which enforces the milestone law where you live.

faq.q: What is spalling on a condo balcony?
faq.a: Spalling is when pieces of the concrete surface crack loose, flake off or fall away. On Florida buildings it often happens when steel bars inside the concrete rust after salt and moisture reach them. Only an engineer or architect can say how serious a particular spot is.

faq.q: Are rust stains on concrete a structural problem?
faq.a: They can be a sign that the steel inside is rusting, but a stain alone does not tell you how serious it is. Photograph it, report it to your board or manager in writing, and ask that the association's engineer look at it.

faq.q: Do cracks mean my Florida condo will fail its milestone inspection?
faq.a: Not automatically. Section 553.899 leaves cracks out of the definition of substantial structural deterioration unless the engineer or architect doing the inspection decides they are a sign of it. If Phase 1 finds substantial structural deterioration, a Phase 2 inspection is required.

faq.q: Who do I tell if I see concrete falling off my condo building?
faq.a: Tell the board or manager in writing right away and keep clear of the area. The association's engineer can evaluate it. If you believe a condition is unsafe, you can also contact your local building department, which enforces Florida's milestone inspection law.
